findings.title: File read of the saved notebook can fail confusingly if pathA is empty or the save did not complete
findings.message: `must(t, e)` aborts the test with the raw error, but the failure is indistinguishable from a genuine IO problem versus a setup bug (e.g. pathA empty because `State().Path` was not populated). When this fires, debugging "why did reading a temp file fail" is much harder than it needs to be.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the error with context so failures are self-diagnosing:
findings.evidence:
data, e := os.ReadFile(pathA)
	must(t, e)
	saved, e := DecodeNotebook(data)
	must(t, e)
	if !reflect.DeepEqual(saved.Notes, expectedA) {
		t.Fatal("first saved notebook differs from approved content")
	}

findings.title: Update discards the expected note content, weakening the exact-content comparison
findings.message: The test claims to verify "distinct exact Unicode notebooks, including CRLF", but `id` is the only key used to update the note, and the expected content is captured from `f[i].model.Items()` immediately after the update inside the same closure. If `Update` (or a subsequent save/load) normalizes line endings or re-encodes content, the captured `expectedA` and the decoded file would both contain the same normalized value, so the CRLF/Unicode claim is never actually exercised as a distinguisher; the assertion is tautological against any transformation applied before `Items()` is read.
findings.suggestion: Capture the expected values from the literal strings used for the update rather than from `f[i].model.Items()`, so any normalization performed by the model or the save/load round trip is actually detected.
findings.evidence: must(t, f[i].model.Update(id, title, "Exact café 日本語\r\n"+title))

finding.title: Inner loop variable `title2` is unused and shadowed by `titles[i2]`
finding.message: The inner range loop declares `i2` and `title2`, then immediately discards `title2` and re-derives the title via `titles[i2]`. This is confusing, and `title2` is unused (Go will reject unused loop variables? No — Go does not reject unused range variables, but linters and reviewers will flag it as dead). More importantly, the indirection through `titles[i2]` makes the relationship between the loop and the data opaque and easy to get wrong if the slices ever diverge.
finding.suggestion: Use the range variables directly and drop the redundant re-indexing:
finding.evidence:
id2, e := f[i2].model.Add()
			must(t, f[i2].model.Update(id2, titles[i2], ""))
